project.name: opensourcedating
project.name_note: Working title. No name has been chosen yet.
project.tagline: An open-source dating app, piloted in Berlin. You search and read profiles instead of swiping, write one thoughtful opening message, and chat end-to-end encrypted.
project.stage_detail: Phase 1 of 7: planning and building. No app code yet; the first tests use bots, then fake profiles only.
project.note: Decided means Hendrik decided it. Planned means agreed as a later step but not designed yet. Guess means a working assumption or a recommendation still waiting for a decision. Open means nobody has decided yet.

intro.what: A free, open-source dating app for Android and iOS. It starts as a pilot in Berlin on one server run by a small non-profit, and later grows into a network: one server program run by many operators, where only vetted operators run the servers that can read search data. No single company owns the people who use it.

why.title: Dating apps are built to keep you swiping
why.text: Card stacks, endless feeds and hidden ranking reward quick judgements on a photo and time spent in the app, not good conversations.

why.title: Visibility is for sale
why.text: Boosts, paid likes and premium tiers decide who gets seen. We don't sell visibility at all.

why.title: The data is about as sensitive as data gets
why.text: Sexuality, gender, location and private chats. Leaks and data sales have hurt real people, queer users most of all. We treat all of it as special-category data under GDPR.

why.title: Nobody can check what the apps do
why.text: The big apps are closed. Ours is public code anyone can read, test and run, with no patents.

principles.title: Search, don't swipe
principles.text: Filter and browse a results list, like old OkCupid. Read profiles, compare, come back later. No card stack, no endless feed.

principles.title: One opening message
principles.text: Anyone can write one text-only message to anyone they can see, with a small weekly allowance. A reply starts the conversation; silence is a normal no.

principles.title: Chats only the two of you can read
principles.text: End-to-end encrypted with libsignal (the Signal protocol). The server passes messages on and deletes them once delivered.

principles.title: Location you choose
principles.text: No GPS. You pick a home area on a Berlin map at the precision you want. Others see travel time by public transport, never a distance.

principles.title: No hidden ranking, nothing for sale
principles.text: You choose the sort order. No paid boosts, no "who viewed me", no "online now".

principles.title: Safety built in from day one
principles.text: Hide, block and report (reporting always blocks), a separate safety service, verifiable reports, optional photo verification on the phone and an 18+ check that stores only the result.

principles.title: Open source, run by a non-profit
principles.text: Public repo, no patents. A Berlin non-profit association (e.V.), being founded now, runs the pilot server.

principles.title: Test data until it's reviewed
principles.text: The first pilot uses fake profiles and labelled test bots. Real users only after a human security review and a data protection assessment.

journey.title: Sign up without a password
journey.text: A passkey first, a one-time email code as the fallback (Ory Kratos). No password and no phone number. You confirm you are 18 or older. Your account gets a random ID with no server name in it, bound to your phone's key; your email is never shown or used as a key. Recovering the account on a new phone waits 24 hours and tells the old phone, which can cancel it.

journey.title: Write your profile
journey.text: Long-form texts, interest tags and photos. You pick any number of gender labels and choose exactly one search group (woman, man or non-binary); orientation is an optional label, hidden by default and never a filter. Your profile stays hidden until you publish it, and publishing shows the privacy choices and asks for consent. Openness (mono, open, poly) and relationship status are their own fields. Which relationship dimensions replace "intensity" is still being designed.

journey.title: Pick your home area
journey.text: Tap your area on a Berlin map and choose how precisely it is stored: about 1.5 km by default, or 500 m, or your district. Only that area is kept, never a history. You can move it at most once a day and four times a month, so nobody can use it to pin you down. A finer location is only ever shared phone to phone inside a conversation.

journey.title: Search and browse
journey.text: Set filters (travel time, age, search groups and "looking for", relationship type, recently active, photo verified, interest tags) and browse 20 results a page. Search groups are two-way: you only see people who are also looking for someone like you. Age is two-way with a 5-year margin, and a symbol shows when you are outside someone's range. Results show the exact age, never the date of birth. Profile texts are searchable only for people who opt in.

journey.title: Write one opening message
journey.text: Text only, no links. You get 5 a week (2 for new or unverified accounts), so you choose carefully. Unanswered messages disappear after 30 days, with no read receipts, and the allowance comes back. An inbox holds at most 15 unanswered messages; after that senders see a "full" notice, never a number.

journey.title: A reply starts the conversation
journey.text: From then on you chat end-to-end encrypted. The server only ever holds encrypted messages, and only until they arrive. Either of you can end the conversation at any time.

journey.title: Stay safe
journey.text: Hide someone from your results, block them (silent, both ways) or report them (which always blocks too), choosing from seven reasons. Child sexual abuse material and threats to life are handled immediately, the rest within 24 hours. Moderators can verify reported messages without the server ever reading chats.

journey.title: Leave whenever you want
journey.text: Deleting your account takes effect at once, after you sign in again; backups expire after 30 days and photos are crypto-shredded. Inactive profiles are hidden after 3 months and deleted after 12, with warnings. Export your data by request during the test, in the app before real users (phase 5).

not_building: Swiping, card stacks or one-at-a-time decisions
An endless feed (results are paginated and the list ends)
Photos, links or read receipts in opening messages

mockups.title: Search
mockups.note: The design doc leaves list vs. grid open, and specifies a non-empty state for the early pilot -- shown as three options.

mockups.title: Write & save
mockups.note: One opening message per profile, a reply starts the conversation, and a private Save list nobody is told about.

mockups.title: Chat
mockups.note: A conversation opens once the recipient replies to an opening message; the safety-controls layout isn't designed yet.

mockups.title: Profile
mockups.note: Three profile views (yours, theirs, and the preview card in results), none final. Actions on someone else's profile are Write, Save, Hide, Block and Report.

architecture.summary: Two stages. The Berlin pilot runs on one server operated by an accountable legal entity, because search, blocking, bans and moderation need someone who can enforce rules and act as the GDPR controller. Later, one server program runs on two levels: sealed servers run only by vetted operators, and plain servers that anyone in the EU can run under a signed agreement. Stage 1 is built so stage 2 needs no rewrite.

stages.title: Stage 1: one server (Berlin pilot)
stages.summary: Phones talk to a single open-source server in Germany. It handles sign-in, profiles, search by home area, opening-message allowances and the chat relay. Bans, reports and verification live in a separate safety service. Chats are end-to-end encrypted; the relay deletes each message once it is delivered.

stages.title: Stage 2: one program on two levels (later)
stages.summary: Every server runs the same program. The sealed level runs inside hardware enclaves that phones check before trusting them; it holds the small search cards and runs admission, ban and photo checks. Only vetted operators run it, in professional data centres, under a signed agreement. The plain level only stores and relays encrypted data (profile items, photos, messages); anyone in the EU who signs the operator agreement can run it. No shards, no home servers: profiles are not split across servers and accounts belong to no server. A shared ban list keeps a banned person out everywhere. Who holds profile content keys is still open.

groundwork: Account IDs that don't depend on any one server: a random 128-bit code with no server name, bound to the phone's key by a certificate.
Safety data (bans, reports, verification) and admission run as their own services with an API, so they can move to the sealed level.
Profile and photo storage sit behind one interface (put, get, delete an item, able to hold ciphertext), so it can move to the plain level later.
Search reads only the search card fields through its own interface, never the full profile.
Every chat message carries a franking tag, so reports stay verifiable across servers.

decisions.choice: One central open-source server
decisions.why: Search, blocking and moderation need an accountable operator; one shared pool helps the small pilot.
decisions.alternatives: Federation from day one, pure phone-to-phone

decisions.choice: React Native + Expo, libsignal in our own native Kotlin/Swift module
decisions.why: Fastest for one developer on both platforms; every option needs a native libsignal bridge anyway, and that module is reusable and fundable.
decisions.alternatives: Flutter, Kotlin Multiplatform, fully native Kotlin + Swift

decisions.choice: Ory Kratos with passkeys first, email codes as fallback; 24 h recovery wait with a cancel notice to the old phone
decisions.why: No passwords and no custom auth code to get wrong. The waiting period stops someone with access to the email inbox from silently taking over an account.
decisions.alternatives: Phone number, own auth

decisions.choice: Random opaque 128-bit ID, no @server, not derived from a key, bound to the device key by a certificate. One phone per account and no chat backup.
decisions.why: Stable when a phone is lost, ties nobody to a server, and works with Kratos now and the stage 2 design later.
decisions.alternatives: id@server, an ID made from a phone key

decisions.choice: libsignal end-to-end encryption, opening messages included; relay deletes after delivery
decisions.why: Nothing readable or lasting on the server; works when the other phone is offline.
decisions.alternatives: Matrix (keeps history on servers), pure phone-to-phone (no offline delivery, leaks IPs)

decisions.choice: Bans, reports, verification and photo hashes in a separate service with its own database and API
decisions.why: Lets stage 2 share one ban list between servers without a rewrite.
decisions.alternatives: Inside the main database

decisions.choice: Message franking in the message format from v1
decisions.why: Moderators can check reported messages are genuine without the server reading chats.
decisions.alternatives: Trusting screenshots

decisions.choice: Optional on-device liveness and face comparison with its own consent; the server gets only a signed yes or no with app attestation
decisions.why: Scales without staff and keeps biometric data on the phone. The DPO and lawyer confirm the consent design before real users (phase 5).
decisions.alternatives: Human check of a requested-pose photo, a vendor service

decisions.choice: Seven report reasons; CSAM and threats to life immediately, under-18 within a few hours, the rest within 24 h; Hendrik plus one backup, both with escalation contacts
decisions.why: Clear targets for the worst cases and no single point of failure during the pilot. The backup is not named yet.
decisions.alternatives: Volunteer moderators, no fixed targets

decisions.choice: Self-chosen home area, stored at about 1.5 km by default (500 m or district selectable), no GPS, changes rate-limited
decisions.why: The stored precision is all an attacker can ever learn, so the default is a neighbourhood, not a few streets. Finer location only goes phone to phone in a conversation.
decisions.alternatives: GPS radius, 500 m default, district only

decisions.choice: Filtered search, no swiping, user-chosen sort
decisions.why: Better decisions, no dark patterns, no swipe-patent exposure.
decisions.alternatives: Card stack

decisions.choice: Interest tags (fixed list plus own short tags) and opt-in searchable profile texts: off by default, reciprocal, search words never logged; saved searches run on the phone
decisions.why: Free text for everyone would need readable texts on the server and would find labels people chose to hide.
decisions.alternatives: Free-text search over all profiles, no keyword search

decisions.choice: Search groups two-way; age two-way with a 5-year margin; travel time one-way; a symbol on the tile when you're outside someone's range
decisions.why: Cuts unwanted messages without hiding people over small differences. Accepted leak: symbols hint where the other person's limits are.
decisions.alternatives: Age and travel time both two-way, only search groups two-way

decisions.choice: Any number of gender labels plus exactly one search group (woman, man, non-binary); openness and relationship status as own one-way fields; orientation optional, hidden, never a filter; intentions stored as a list; exact age shown, never the date of birth; profile hidden until first published
decisions.why: Filters need as little Art. 9 data as possible, and nobody becomes visible before they have seen the privacy choices. Relationship type is still open.
decisions.alternatives: Gender as the filter, orientation as a filter, age bands

decisions.choice: 5 opening messages a week (2 for accounts under two weeks old or unverified); allowance returned when a message expires unanswered after 30 days; inbox cap of 15 unanswered messages, adjustable, with a "full" notice and no number
decisions.why: Limits mass messaging and overloaded inboxes without a hidden ranking; numbers are tuned with pilot data. An allowance relative to how many profiles fit your search is a future idea, not decided.
decisions.alternatives: No inbox cap, allowance never returned

decisions.choice: Self-declared date of birth for the fake-data phases (2 to 4); only the result is ever stored. The stronger check is chosen before real users (phase 5) (recommended: German eID age-only query, ID scan through an EU vendor as the fallback)
decisions.why: No ID scans or face data on the server. The DSA guidelines expect verification for high-risk services; the choice is deferred until real users are near and can change behind one interface.
decisions.alternatives: Selfie estimate only, human video check, ID upload

decisions.choice: Instant deletion with a hold under open reports; 30-day backups with a replayed deletion list; photos crypto-shredded; only a ban record kept after a ban, 2 years; inactive accounts hidden at 3 months, deleted at 12
decisions.why: Smallest data set that still keeps bans effective. The lawyer confirms the 2-year period and the basis for the open-report hold.
decisions.alternatives: Delayed deletion with undo, keeping reports against non-banned accounts

decisions.choice: None during the fake-data phases (2 to 4); before real users (phase 5), keyed IP hashes (key rotated daily, kept 7 days) in the reverse proxy, Kratos, relay and safety service
decisions.why: Spots sign-up farms within a week without storing addresses that reveal where people are.
decisions.alternatives: Raw IPs for 7 days, no logging at all

decisions.choice: An EU-based transactional email provider with a DPA, minimal content, no app name in the subject if possible; provider not chosen yet (Scaleway, Lettermint or Brevo compared)
decisions.why: An email alone can reveal that someone uses a dating app, so it should say as little as possible and stay with an EU processor.
decisions.alternatives: A US email service, own mail server

decisions.choice: Own small Hetzner server in Germany, separate from anything else
decisions.why: Cheap, EU-hosted, isolated from other services. Set up and locked down; nothing deployed yet.
decisions.alternatives: An existing personal server

decisions.choice: Berlin e.V. (non-profit association), founded now with seven founders, before any public announcement or grant press
decisions.why: Someone has to be the GDPR controller and DSA hosting provider, and the project is already public, so liability should move off one person early.
decisions.alternatives: Found it only before real users (phase 5), gGmbH, UG

decisions.choice: AGPL-3.0-or-later with a section 7 additional permission for app store distribution (LICENSE-EXCEPTION)
decisions.why: App store terms conflict with the AGPL; adding the permission is easy now while the copyright holders are few. The lawyer is asked once about libsignal on iOS.
decisions.alternatives: No exception, relicensing store builds

decisions.choice: One server program on two levels: sealed level run by vetted operators in data centres; plain level open to anyone in the EU who signs the operator agreement. No home servers, one shared ban list
decisions.why: Enclaves can be broken by someone with physical access, and every operator processes Art. 9 data, so the servers that read data need vetted, contracted operators. Storing and relaying ciphertext can be open to more people under the same agreement.
decisions.alternatives: Fully open servers, vetted servers only, groups of servers agreeing on each person's data

decisions.choice: Profile content encrypted on the phone and stored on plain servers; only minimal search cards are readable, inside the sealed level
decisions.why: Plain operators only ever hold ciphertext, and an enclave break exposes little. Splitting profiles into k-of-n pieces is dropped: content is already encrypted, so it added a lot of work for little privacy.
decisions.alternatives: Encrypted pieces spread across servers (k-of-n), each server keeping its users' full profiles

decisions.choice: Open: if the sealed level holds every profile's content key, an enclave break exposes full profiles. Accept that openly in the threat model and DPIA, or move to proxy re-encryption before stage 2
decisions.why: Decides how much an enclave break can expose.
decisions.alternatives: Sealed level holds the keys, proxy re-encryption

topics.intro: Every key feature and rule is reviewed one topic at a time before prototype code is written, costliest to change later first. Each decided topic has its own spec file.

items.title: Accounts and identity
points: Passkeys first, email codes as the fallback; no passwords, no phone number.
The account ID is a random 128-bit code with no server name, bound to the phone's key by a certificate. Email is never a key.
Recovery on a new phone waits 24 hours and tells the old phone, which can cancel it.
One phone per account in the pilot, no chat backup. A lost phone gets the account back, but not old chats.
Login codes go through an EU email provider with a DPA and as little content as possible; the provider is not chosen yet.

items.title: Profile data model: gender, orientation and "looking for"
points: You pick any number of gender labels and exactly one search group: woman, man or non-binary. Only search group and age are two-way; relationship types, openness (mono, open, poly) and relationship status are your own filters only.
Orientation is an optional label, hidden by default and never a filter. No trans filter in the fake-data phases.
"Looking for" is stored as a list of intentions; the first app shows one.
Optional "how soon do you like to meet" field; narrative prompts instead of a blank "About me"; photos carry a self-declared age band or a "taken in the app" mark.
A new profile stays hidden until you publish it; the publish step shows the privacy choices and asks for the Art. 9 consent.
Still open: which dimensions replace "intensity" (draft only).

items.title: Who sees what, and when
points: Six steps: not findable, search preview, full profile, opening message, conversation, shared by choice. Details only get more precise when the person described acts.
Exact age in previews; the date of birth is never shown. Age is two-way with a 5-year margin, travel time one-way, with a symbol when you are outside someone's range.
A fit checklist on every profile shows why someone is in your results, using only fields they made visible.
"Only people I write to" mode and a pause switch, free for everyone; photos can be conversation-only.
A finer location is shared only phone to phone inside a conversation.
No secret "both interested" signal. Compatibility questions with a visible score: later.

items.title: Opening messages and conversations
points: One text-only opening message per person; a reply starts the conversation.
5 a week, 2 for new or unverified accounts; the allowance comes back when a message expires unanswered after 30 days.
Inboxes hold at most 15 unanswered messages (adjustable); senders then see a "full" notice, never a number.
Opening messages are end-to-end encrypted too; "no links" is enforced on the recipient's phone.
Either person can end a conversation; after that neither can write again, but it isn't a block.
Recipients sort and filter their own inbox; ending a conversation sends a short, kind fixed message by default.

A "Suggest meeting" message (what, where, when) with yes, counter or not yet; a private nudge after a week of writing; quiet chats archive themselves after 30 days; "waiting for your reply" is visible only to you.

items.title: Safety and moderation
points: Hide, block (silent, both ways) and report (always blocks). Reported people hear only when action is taken, with reasons and appeal.
Seven report reasons. CSAM and threats to life handled immediately, under-18 within a few hours, the rest within 24 hours.
Hendrik plus one backup moderate the pilot, both with escalation contacts; the backup is not named yet.
Optional photo verification runs on the phone; only a signed yes or no reaches the server.
The verified badge shows its month and is renewed yearly; a soft report sub-reason for stale photos; a private "did you meet, did you feel safe" check-in that feeds safety only.
Separate safety service from day one; verifiable reports through message franking. Ban evasion via hashed email, photo-file hashes and device signals, never face recognition.

items.title: Location
points: No GPS; a self-chosen home area, stored only at the precision the user picked: about 1.5 km by default, or 500 m, or district.
Home area changes at most once a day and four times in 30 days.
Travel-time bands by public transport, never distances. A finer location only goes phone to phone in a conversation.

items.title: Photos and profile storage
points: Decided: photo verification runs on the phone (topic 5), and stage 2 keeps profile content encrypted on plain servers, with no pieces split across servers (topic 12).
Still open: how photos are checked before they go public, and a conversation-only tier (see Open questions).

items.title: Age check (18+)
points: Self-declared date of birth for the fake-data phases (2 to 4).
Which stronger check is deferred until before real users (phase 5). Recommended: German eID age-only query, ID scan through an EU vendor as the fallback; the EU age app once available.
Only the result is stored, never a selfie or an ID.

items.title: Deletion, retention and export
points: Deletion takes effect at once (after signing in again), held only while a report is open; 30-day backups, photos crypto-shredded.
After a ban only the ban record is kept, 2 years pending the lawyer.
Export by request during the test, in the app before real users (phase 5). Inactive accounts hidden at 3 months, deleted at 12, with warnings.
No IP logging in the fake-data phases (2 to 4); before real users (phase 5) only keyed IP hashes, kept 7 days.

items.title: Search limits
points: 20 results a page, and the list ends.
Interest tags instead of free-text keywords; profile texts searchable only for people who opt in (off by default, reciprocal). Search words are never logged.
Saved searches and alerts run on the phone.
50 full-profile views a day for new accounts, 200 after two weeks, to slow down scrapers. "Hide" lasts until you undo it.

items.title: Test bots
points: Every bot and its data is flagged and wipeable in one go; testers see a "test bot" badge.
Generated photos only. Bots run on a separate machine through the public API, rate limits on.
Attack bots try to locate users and copy profiles; the tests fail if they succeed.

items.title: Stage 2: one server program on two levels
points: The sealed level runs in enclaves that phones check; it holds search cards and runs admission, ban and photo checks. Only vetted operators run it, in data centres, under a signed agreement.
The plain level stores and relays encrypted data; anyone in the EU who signs the operator agreement can run it.
No shards and no home servers. One shared ban list.
Still open: who holds profile content keys, where sealed servers run, the protocol between servers and deletion across servers.

items.title: Common frustrations: ghosting, chats that go nowhere, stale photos, AI chats
points: Research: in Germany ghosting or no reply is the top frustration (54%, forsa for KKH 2025); for 54% a contact rarely becomes a real meeting (Bitkom 2025); 19% have used AI-written chat texts.
From chat to meeting: a "Suggest meeting" button in the chat, a "how soon do you like to meet" profile field, a private nudge after a week, a private safety check-in after a meeting.

Going silent: ending kindly is the one-tap default; quiet chats archive themselves after 30 days; only you see which chats wait on you; reply or end before writing to someone new once more than 8 wait.
Current photos and specific profiles: photo age bands, a dated verification badge renewed yearly, in-app camera photos, narrative prompts.
AI-written chats: the app never offers AI writing help; the other person's profile sits beside the text field with one tip; a community agreement asks people to write their own messages.
Every nudge is shown only to the person it concerns, never as a push notification, and can be switched off.

other.title: Pilot scope
other.text: Berlin, city-wide. Phase 3 is a test with the Berlin tech scene using fake profiles; phase 4 brings in the queer community, still with fake profiles, once gender, preference and safety features are solid. Real profiles start in phase 5.

other.title: Build our own
other.text: We build a new app rather than fork Alovoa, the existing open-source dating app, and borrow ideas from it.

other.title: Open and unpatented
other.text: Public repository from the start, no patents.

other.title: Non-profit founded now
other.text: The Berlin e.V. is founded now with seven founders, before any public announcement or grant press, so liability moves off one person early.

other.title: App store licence exception
other.text: AGPL-3.0-or-later with a section 7 additional permission for app store distribution (LICENSE-EXCEPTION). The lawyer is asked once about libsignal on iOS.

other.title: Sign off every commit (DCO)
other.text: Every commit carries a Developer Certificate of Origin sign-off, enforced by a CI check on pull requests (see CONTRIBUTING.md).

questions: Describe relationship types beyond the intention with the draft dimensions (openness, length, intensity): openness two-way, length and intensity your own filter only?
Two tiers: public profile on the server, conversation-only content sent after a reply?
Volunteer photo checking for low-risk questions?

items: Who holds profile content keys: accept that an enclave break exposes full profiles, or move to proxy re-encryption first.
Where sealed servers run: confidential VMs at a large cloud, or dedicated hardware.
Which fields the readable search card holds.
Which protocol servers use to talk to each other.
How deletion reaches every server (GDPR Art. 17(2)), and whether the operator agreement makes each level a processor or a joint controller (lawyer).
Name the backup moderator for the pilot.
Lawyer confirms the 2-year ban-record period and the basis for holding accounts under open reports.
DPO and lawyer confirm the consent design for photo verification before real users (phase 5).
Does the open-source Kratos support passkeys in native apps? A one-day spike before building login.
Which EU email provider sends login codes (Scaleway, Lettermint or Brevo).
Rate limits on search requests.
Which stronger age check before real users (phase 5): German eID age-only query, or an ID scan through an EU vendor.
Who runs and pays for the server before the e.V. exists.
Lawyer: libsignal (AGPL) on iOS under the app store licence exception.

roadmap.title: Plan and build
roadmap.who: Hendrik and the e.V. founders. No users.
items: Spec review: settle the costly decisions first.
Found the Berlin e.V. with seven founders, before any public announcement.
Funding applications: NLnet (3 Nov 2026) and the Prototype Fund (30 Nov 2026).
Build the prototype: server, safety service, sign-in, relay, app with the libsignal module, test bots.

roadmap.title: Server and bot test
roadmap.who: Test bots only, all data generated and bot-flagged.
items: Deploy to the pilot server in Germany.
Load test with many bots; attack bots try scraping, spam, allowance abuse and ban evasion.
Restore and deletion drills; wipe all bot data in one go.

roadmap.title: Tech testers
roadmap.who: Invited people from the Berlin tech scene, using fake profiles, who also review the code.
items: Real people try search, opening messages, block and report.
Code review and security reports.
Apps via TestFlight and Google Play internal testing.

roadmap.title: Community test
roadmap.who: A small invited community, starting with the Berlin queer scene, still with fake profiles.
items: Check the data model, wording and safety tools with the people who need them most.
Being in this group can itself reveal something real, so the data protection check is redone first.
All fake data is wiped at the end.

roadmap.title: Real profiles, selected users
roadmap.who: Invite-only waves with real profiles, kept balanced.
items: Before it starts: external security review, data protection impact assessment and external DPO, stronger age check, keyed IP hashes, export in the app, named moderators.
Real dating in small waves; limits tuned with real use.

roadmap.title: Berlin, open to all
items: Public store listings in Germany and the EU.
Recruit by district and events so every area has enough people.
Build stage 2.

roadmap.title: Beyond Berlin
items: Most likely through stage 2: one server program on two levels, sealed servers run by vetted operators, plain servers anyone in the EU can run under a signed agreement.

suggestions.intro: Recommendations from the research that still need a decision. Have an idea of your own? Open an issue on GitHub.

items.title: Apply to the Prototype Fund
items.summary: Pays developer time on public-interest open source (up to 47,500 € for one person). Current round closes 30 Nov 2026.

items.title: Apply to NLnet for one component
items.summary: For example the libsignal module for React Native/Expo or the encrypted chat relay. Deadline 3 Nov 2026, noon CET.

items.title: Write down why the fake-data phases need no DPO
items.summary: Holds only while phases 2 to 4 really use fake data. A DPIA and an external DPO are needed once real dating data comes in.

items.title: Human security review before any real data
items.summary: Keep the pilot on test data until a person has reviewed the server, the relay and the sign-in setup.

items.title: Invite-only waves, balanced and recruited at events
items.summary: Gate waves so the gender and orientation mix stays balanced; open an area only once new users would see real profiles on day one.

items.title: Contact the Alovoa maintainer
items.summary: Report their encryption issue privately through their SECURITY.md and ask about sharing pieces later.

items.title: Register the name as a trademark
items.summary: Once a name is chosen: German mark at the DPMA (around 290 €) before phase 5 (real profiles); consider an EU mark if stage 2 reaches other countries.
